mappings.note: Names c in y=mx+c the y-intercept. LO-5 is the only outcome covering the y-intercept; LO-6 concerns what CHANGING the intercept does to two lines.
Defines the case 'increases by the same fixed amount each period' as linear growth, which is LO-3's own language. Not C-3.2-LO-1: no table of values is given to test.
Plant 12 cm growing 3 cm a week is modelled as 3w+12 and used at w=8 -- a rising-quantity model, LO-3. The prediction step is subordinate to building the growth model.

Tests the classic linear-growth misconception (doubling time doubles the quantity, which fails whenever the intercept is non-zero). That is knowing what a linear-growth model does, LO-3, not slope-reading.
'The graph of a linear polynomial is always a straight line' is the second clause of LO-4 -- why the points lie on a straight line. LO-5 would require slope or intercept to be read.
Builds a three-row table for y=3x-2 and describes the resulting graph: LO-4's 'draws the graph of a linear relationship from a table of values' precisely.

Both statements concern the straight-line/y=mx+c correspondence, which is LO-4's territory. Cited to LO-4 rather than LO-5 because the claim under test is about lines as a class, not about reading one line's slope.
'Two points are enough to draw a linear graph' is a fact about constructing the graph, LO-4. Nothing is interpreted, so not LO-5.

Two lines with the same slope 2 and different intercepts, and the comparison is the point of the item -- LO-6 ('same slope give parallel lines ... effect of changing the intercept'). LO-4 covers only the table-to-graph step, which is here just the method.
A construction task: table, plot, draw and label y=2x-4, marking both axis crossings. LO-4 is the drawing outcome; the intercepts are marked, not interpreted, so LO-5 is not the target.
Equal slopes imply parallel -- the first clause of LO-6 verbatim.
Asks WHY equal slopes with unequal intercepts never meet (constant non-zero vertical gap). LO-6 asks for exactly that explanation, where LO-5 would only require naming the slope.
Assesses the converse error: same intercept does not force the same line. LO-6's 'predicts the effect of changing the intercept' is the outcome being probed, with slope held as the discriminator.
Different slopes must intersect exactly once -- the contrapositive of LO-6's parallel-lines statement. Still LO-6 and not LO-5, because two lines are compared.

Three lines on one diagram, two parallel and one with opposite slope, used to explain what slope and intercept each control. LO-6 for the parallel pair and the intercept shift; LO-5 for the 'what does each number control' reading. LO-4 is only the drawing method.
Reads the meaning of a negative slope (y falls as x rises) for a single line -- slope interpretation, LO-5. Cited here rather than LO-3 because no real situation is attached to make it a decay model.
500-25t is linear decay, which LO-3 names, and the second half asks for the domain limit t<=20 where the model stops describing the tank. That is modelling judgement, not graph reading.
Screens candidates for whether they are polynomials in one variable at all -- LO-2's distinguishing test. LO-1 assumes you already have a polynomial and asks its degree.
Links the constant first difference in a table (LO-1's test) to the slope of the line (LO-5). The item exists to connect the two, so both are cited rather than choosing one.
Differences 4,4,5,4: apply the constant-difference test and reject linearity. This is LO-1 exactly; no rule ax+b is asked for, so not LO-2.
Method question on deciding linearity from a table, including unequal x-spacing and measurement noise -- an extended form of LO-1's difference test.
Fixed 30 plus 12 per km written as 12d+30: building a linear model of a charging situation, LO-3. Nothing is predicted or interpreted, so not LO-2 or LO-5.

Competency: two competing linear models are equated (200+2n = 100+4n), solved, and a recommendation is drawn for each side of n=50. That 'draws conclusions about a situation being modelled' clause is in the competency, not in any single LO; LO-3 stops at writing one model.

A three-part synthesis: what a linear polynomial is (degree one, a!=0 -- LO-1), that its graph is a straight line (LO-4), and what slope and intercept mean in a real situation (LO-5). Each part carries its own marks.
P=150n-9000 analysed: the 150 as contribution per item and -9000 as fixed cost is LO-5 interpretation; the break-even calculation is the competency's solve-and-conclude step, which no LO here covers.

Assembles y=-2x+7 from the given intercept and slope and then inverts it to find x when y=1 -- writing the rule and using it, LO-2. LO-5 would apply if the slope or intercept had to be read off instead of being handed over.
Competency: the equation to be solved, (4n+500)/n = 6, is not linear, so no linear-polynomial LO applies; it is a contextualised problem solved with an equation, which is what C-3.2 states.

Proves the converse direction of the difference test -- constant first difference over equal steps implies the relation is linear (LO-1's criterion) and yields a rule of the form ax+b (LO-2). Cited to the two algebra LOs rather than CG-2, whose proof examples are about numbers, not about tabulated relations.
